subtopic_detail: Porcelain white vulval plaques with loss of the labia minora and burying of the clitoris in a postmenopausal woman
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a sixty two year old woman who reports two years of vulval itch that is worst at night. She has tried several over the counter antifungal creams and a barrier ointment without benefit, and has recently found intercourse painful at the entrance.

She went through menopause at fifty one and has used no hormone therapy. She has autoimmune hypothyroidism treated with thyroxine. She has had no abnormal cervical screening results and no vaginal discharge.

data_table.Examination: Porcelain white thickened plaques over both labia majora extending to the perineum in a figure of eight pattern, resorption of the labia minora, clitoral hood fused over the clitoris, several linear excoriations, introital narrowing, no discrete nodule or ulcer, vaginal mucosa normal on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: Vulval swab shows no candida and no bacterial pathogen, urinalysis negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe topical oestrogen cream nightly for two weeks then twice weekly as ongoing maintenance therapy
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen treats genitourinary syndrome of menopause, which produces a pale thin vaginal mucosa with dryness rather than thickened white vulval plaques with architectural loss. The normal vaginal mucosa here points away from an oestrogen deficient process. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval skin conditions)

options.text: Prescribe a two week course of oral fluconazole and advise soap avoidance with regular emollient use
options.rationale: Recurrent candidiasis is a reasonable initial thought given the itch, but the swab is negative and repeated antifungal creams have already failed, which is the pattern that should prompt reconsideration. Architectural change of this kind is never caused by candida. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval skin conditions)

options.text: Apply hydrocortisone one per cent ointment twice daily for six weeks and then review the symptomatic response
options.rationale: A mild corticosteroid is insufficient to control this condition and undertreatment allows scarring to progress while giving the impression that steroid has been tried. The vulva tolerates potent preparations well, so potency is not the limiting factor. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for surgical division of the fused clitoral hood and release of the introital narrowing before medical therapy
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for persistent functional problems after the inflammation has been medically controlled, because operating on active disease risks recurrent fusion and koebnerisation at the incision. Medical control comes first in almost every case. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval skin conditions)

options.text: Apply a potent topical corticosteroid ointment in a reducing regimen over three months with planned clinical review
options.rationale: Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid is first line for lichen sclerosus, typically nightly for a month then tapering to alternate nights and twice weekly, and it both relieves symptoms and slows further architectural loss. Planned review matters because long term maintenance reduces scarring and lowers the risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulval skin conditions)

explanation.summary: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory vulval dermatosis with a bimodal incidence in prepubertal girls and postmenopausal women, and it is strongly associated with other autoimmune disease, particularly thyroid disease. The characteristic appearance is porcelain white atrophic or thickened skin in a figure of eight distribution around the vulva and anus, with progressive architectural change including resorption of the labia minora, burying of the clitoris under a fused hood, and introital narrowing. It is frequently misdiagnosed as thrush for years, and repeated failed antifungal treatment is a common part of the history. Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid is first line and is continued as maintenance rather than stopped once symptoms settle, because ongoing treatment reduces both scarring and malignant transformation. Around four to five per cent of women develop vulval squamous cell carcinoma, which is why any persistent nodule, ulcer or thickened area needs biopsy.
key_points: Figure of eight white plaques with loss of labia minora and clitoral burying are the defining findings
Strong association with autoimmune disease, especially thyroid disease, supports the diagnosis
Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid is first line, with maintenance rather than symptomatic use only
Long term steroid maintenance reduces both progressive scarring and malignant transformation
Around four to five per cent develop vulval squamous cell carcinoma, so new lesions need biopsy
explanation.pearls: A 30 g tube of ultrapotent corticosteroid ointment should last a woman with vulval lichen sclerosus around twelve weeks on a standard reducing regimen, so a tube finished in three weeks signals overuse and one lasting a year signals undertreatment.

subtopic_detail: Third painful fluctuant swelling at the posterior introitus in eighteen months after two previous incision and drainage procedures
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a twenty nine year old woman with three days of increasing pain and swelling at the entrance to the vagina on the left. She cannot sit comfortably and has been walking with a limp.

She has had two similar episodes in the past eighteen months, each treated in the emergency department with incision and drainage under local anaesthetic, and each recurring within a few months. She is otherwise well, is afebrile, and her last cervical screening test was normal two years ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 37.3 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant swelling of 4 cm at the posterior aspect of the left labium majus displacing the introitus medially, overlying skin erythematous and pointing, no induration extending into the perineum, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, no vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: Self collected vaginal swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea sent, result pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of this episode?

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin with metronidazole for seven days and review her in the clinic after the course finishes
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone do not resolve a tense pointing collection, because the problem is an obstructed duct under pressure rather than surrounding cellulitis. Drainage is the therapeutic step and antibiotics are adjunctive at most. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Perform simple incision and drainage under local anaesthetic and arrange follow up with her general practitioner
options.rationale: Simple incision allows the skin edges to reappose within days so the duct reoccludes, which is precisely why she has presented for a third time. Repeating a procedure with a known high recurrence rate does not address the underlying obstruction. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess)

options.text: Aspirate the collection with a wide bore needle under local anaesthetic and send the aspirate for bacterial culture
options.rationale: Needle aspiration empties the cavity without creating a lasting drainage tract, giving the highest recurrence rate of the available options. It is reasonable only as temporising relief when definitive treatment is genuinely unavailable. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess)

options.text: Insert a balloon tipped word catheter after incision, leaving it in place for four weeks to form an epithelialised tract
options.rationale: With recurrent disease the objective is a permanent drainage tract rather than a further one off evacuation, and a word catheter left for around four weeks allows the tract to epithelialise so the gland can drain in the long term. It is a local anaesthetic office procedure with recurrence rates far below those of simple incision. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess)

options.text: Arrange excision of the gland on the next available elective theatre list and manage the pain with oral analgesia
options.rationale: Excision is reserved for repeated failure of tract forming procedures or when malignancy is suspected, because it carries risks of significant bleeding from the vestibular bulb, scarring and dyspareunia. Waiting for an elective list also leaves an acutely painful collection undrained. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess)

explanation.summary: The Bartholin glands sit at the four and eight o'clock positions of the vestibule and drain through short ducts, and obstruction of the duct produces a cyst that may become secondarily infected to form an abscess. Most are polymicrobial with vaginal and enteric flora, but sexually transmitted infection is tested for because it changes partner management rather than because it dominates the microbiology. The central management principle is that a procedure which simply empties the cavity leaves the obstructed duct intact, so recurrence is high, whereas procedures that create a lasting epithelialised tract, such as word catheter insertion or marsupialisation, have much lower recurrence. Antibiotics are added when there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression rather than routinely. In women over forty a new Bartholin mass warrants biopsy or excision because of the small but real possibility of carcinoma.
key_points: Duct obstruction is the underlying problem, so emptying the cavity alone predicts recurrence
Word catheter or marsupialisation creates an epithelialised tract and markedly reduces recurrence
The word catheter stays in place for around four weeks to allow the tract to form
Antibiotics are added for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression
A new Bartholin mass in a woman over forty requires biopsy to exclude carcinoma
explanation.pearls: A Bartholin cyst that is asymptomatic and small in a woman under forty needs no intervention at all, so the decision to operate is driven by symptoms and recurrence rather than by the presence of the cyst itself.

subtopic_detail: Wedge shaped breast redness with rigors persisting after twenty four hours of effective milk removal and cold packs
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a thirty one year old woman who is sixteen days postpartum and breastfeeding her first baby. She noticed a tender area in the right breast yesterday morning and has been feeding frequently from that side, applying cold packs afterwards and taking regular ibuprofen and paracetamol as advised by the midwife.

Overnight she developed shaking chills and aching limbs. She has a crack at the base of the right nipple which has been present for a week. The baby is feeding every three hours, has plenty of wet nappies and has regained birth weight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Wedge shaped erythema over the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, warm firm and tender with no discrete fluctuant mass, fissure at the base of the right nipple with no surrounding satellite lesions, no axillary lymphadenopathy, left breast normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue conservative measures with effective milk removal and analgesia, and review the following day if unchanged
options.rationale: Conservative management is the correct first step and has now been given a fair trial of twenty four hours without improvement, which is the point at which antibiotics are indicated. Rigors and a temperature of 38.6 degrees Celsius also mark a systemic response rather than simple inflammatory engorgement. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis)

options.text: Prescribe oral flucloxacillin for five to seven days and encourage continued feeding from the affected breast
options.rationale: Mastitis that fails twenty four hours of effective milk removal, or that presents with systemic features and a nipple fissure providing a portal of entry, is treated with an antistaphylococcal antibiotic, and flucloxacillin is the Australian first line agent. Feeding continues from the affected side because milk stasis is what perpetuates the process and the milk is safe for the baby. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin and advise expressing and discarding milk from the right breast until the fever settles
options.rationale: Cefalexin is an acceptable alternative for penicillin allergy, but discarding the milk is wrong on both counts, since the milk is safe and stopping feeds from the affected side worsens stasis. Advice to discard also undermines breastfeeding at a vulnerable point. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis)

options.text: Arrange urgent breast ultrasound and surgical review for drainage of a probable underlying collection
options.rationale: Ultrasound is indicated when a discrete fluctuant mass is present or when symptoms fail to settle after 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics, neither of which applies at this point. Imaging now would delay the treatment that is likely to resolve the problem. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis)

options.text: Prescribe oral fluconazole for ductal candidiasis and advise treating the baby with oral antifungal gel as well
options.rationale: Nipple and ductal candidiasis causes bilateral burning pain radiating through the breast after feeds, without fever, wedge shaped erythema or rigors. Treating for fungal infection here addresses the wrong organism entirely. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Mastitis)

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis begins as inflammation from milk stasis and ductal narrowing rather than as infection, which is why the first response is effective milk removal, cold packs, anti inflammatory analgesia and support with attachment. Antibiotics are added when symptoms fail to improve after about twenty four hours of those measures, when systemic features such as fever and rigors are present, or when a nipple fissure provides an obvious portal of entry. Staphylococcus aureus is the usual organism, so flucloxacillin or dicloxacillin is first line in Australia with cefalexin or clindamycin for penicillin allergy. Continued breastfeeding from the affected side is safe and therapeutic, and abrupt weaning during mastitis increases the risk of abscess formation. Failure to settle within 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics, or a discrete fluctuant mass, prompts ultrasound to look for an abscess requiring aspiration.
key_points: Mastitis starts as inflammation from milk stasis, so effective milk removal is the foundation of treatment
Antibiotics are indicated after 24 hours without improvement, or with systemic features or a nipple fissure
Flucloxacillin is the Australian first line agent, with cefalexin or clindamycin for penicillin allergy
Breastfeeding continues from the affected breast, since abrupt weaning increases abscess risk
Ultrasound is reserved for a fluctuant mass or failure to improve after 48 hours of antibiotics
explanation.pearls: Inflammatory breast cancer can mimic mastitis with erythema and peau d'orange, so any breast inflammation that has not fully resolved after a complete antibiotic course requires imaging regardless of how convincing the lactational story was.

subtopic_detail: Urine loss confined to coughing and netball with no nocturia and a normal post void residual in a woman wanting to avoid surgery
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a forty four year old woman who leaks urine when she coughs, sneezes and plays netball on Thursday nights. She has two children delivered vaginally, the second with forceps, and has noticed the problem worsening over three years.

She wears a liner most days and has stopped playing in the second half of games. She does not wake at night to pass urine, does not get a sudden compelling urge and has never leaked on the way to the toilet. She tells you she would prefer to avoid an operation if there is anything else worth trying.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg/m2, no abdominal mass, demonstrable leak from the urethral meatus on coughing with a full bladder, pelvic floor contraction weak and poorly sustained on digital assessment, no prolapse beyond the hymen on straining, vaginal mucosa well oestrogenised
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for nitrites leucocytes glucose and blood, post void residual 25 mL on bladder scan, three day bladder diary shows six voids daily with average volumes of 320 mL and no nocturia

options.text: Refer for urodynamic studies to characterise the bladder before offering her any specific form of treatment
options.rationale: Urodynamics is reserved for a discordant history and examination, mixed or complicated symptoms, or planned surgery after conservative treatment has failed. The history, demonstrable stress leak and normal diary already agree, so the test would not change the first recommendation. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence)

options.text: Prescribe a low dose vaginal oestrogen pessary twice weekly and review her symptoms in three months time
options.rationale: Vaginal oestrogen helps when there is urogenital atrophy contributing to storage symptoms, and the mucosa here is well oestrogenised in a premenopausal woman. It has little effect on the sphincter and support mechanisms that fail during a cough. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence)

options.text: Arrange supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist for at least three months
options.rationale: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training is first line for stress urinary incontinence and cures or substantially improves symptoms in the majority, with supervision producing markedly better results than a leaflet of exercises. A weak poorly sustained contraction on examination identifies exactly the deficit the programme addresses. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence)

options.text: Start oral solifenacin at night and titrate the dose according to her symptom response over six weeks
options.rationale: Antimuscarinic therapy treats urgency incontinence driven by detrusor overactivity, and this woman has no urgency, no frequency and no nocturia on a three day diary. Prescribing it would produce dry mouth and constipation without addressing the mechanism of her leak. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer to a urogynaecologist for a midurethral sling, given the three year history and effect on her sport
options.rationale: Continence surgery is considered after an adequate trial of supervised conservative therapy, and this woman has specifically asked to avoid an operation if alternatives exist. Mesh procedures also carry regulatory and consent requirements in Australia that make them a considered second line choice. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence)

explanation.summary: Urinary incontinence is classified by the circumstances of leakage, and that classification determines treatment more than any investigation does. Stress incontinence occurs with rises in intra abdominal pressure such as coughing, laughing or exercise, and reflects failure of urethral support and sphincter function, commonly after vaginal birth or instrumental delivery. Urgency incontinence follows a sudden compelling desire to void and reflects detrusor overactivity, often with frequency and nocturia on a bladder diary. Mixed incontinence combines both and is treated according to which symptom bothers the woman most. For pure stress incontinence, supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least three months is first line, with weight loss where relevant, and surgery considered only after that trial has failed.
key_points: Leak confined to coughing, sneezing and exercise with no urgency defines stress incontinence
A three day bladder diary showing normal volumes without nocturia argues against detrusor overactivity
Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least three months is first line and often curative
Supervision by a continence physiotherapist substantially outperforms unsupervised exercises
Urodynamics is reserved for discordant findings, mixed symptoms or planned surgery after failed therapy
explanation.pearls: Around a third of women perform a pelvic floor contraction incorrectly on first assessment, most often by bearing down or recruiting gluteal muscles, which is why digital confirmation of a correct contraction precedes any home exercise programme.

subtopic_detail: New urgency and nocturia in a seventy six year old already taking amitriptyline and oxybutynin with a rising post void residual
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a seventy six year old woman who reports a sudden compelling need to pass urine six or seven times a day and twice at night, with leakage before she reaches the toilet on perhaps two days each week.

She has hypertension, osteoarthritis and insomnia. Her daughter mentions that she has seemed more forgetful over recent months and has had two falls getting up at night. She was started on oxybutynin by a locum four months ago with no improvement, and she has taken amitriptyline for sleep for several years.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no palpable bladder, vaginal mucosa thin and pale with loss of rugae, no prolapse beyond the hymen on straining, no perineal sensory loss, gait slow with a wide base, standardised cognitive score 24 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for nitrites and leucocytes, post void residual 140 mL on bladder scan, three day bladder diary shows nine voids daily with average volumes of 160 mL, serum creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the oxybutynin dose and add a bedtime fluid restriction to address the nocturia specifically
options.rationale: Increasing the dose compounds the anticholinergic load that is already contributing to her cognitive decline, falls and rising residual volume, and the drug has produced no benefit in four months. Escalating a failed medication in a woman with these adverse effects worsens the overall picture. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for intradetrusor botulinum toxin injection as the next escalation of her overactive bladder therapy
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin is a third line option after an adequate trial of conservative therapy and appropriate pharmacotherapy, and it further raises the risk of urinary retention in a woman whose residual is already 140 mL. Escalating before deprescribing skips the reversible contributors. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence)

options.text: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to manage the leakage and prevent further night time falls at home
options.rationale: Long term catheterisation is reserved for retention or intractable incontinence where skin integrity is threatened, and it carries substantial infection and bladder stone risks. It manages the symptom while leaving the medication burden and the treatable bladder dysfunction untouched. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence)

options.text: Cease the oxybutynin and review the amitriptyline, starting supervised bladder training with vaginal oestrogen
options.rationale: Two anticholinergic drugs are together driving cognitive impairment, falls and incomplete emptying, and the failed oxybutynin trial gives no reason to continue it, so reducing anticholinergic burden comes before any escalation. Bladder training is first line for urgency and topical oestrogen improves storage symptoms in a woman with an atrophic vaginal mucosa. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence)

options.text: Arrange urgent cystoscopy and urine cytology to exclude bladder malignancy as a cause of her urgency
options.rationale: Cystoscopy is indicated for visible or persistent non visible haematuria, recurrent infection or suspected malignancy, none of which are present on a negative urinalysis. It would investigate a possibility for which there is currently no evidence. (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary incontinence)

explanation.summary: Overactive bladder in older women is frequently worsened, and sometimes wholly caused, by medications that the woman is already taking, so a medication review precedes escalation of treatment. Anticholinergic burden accumulates across drug classes including bladder antimuscarinics, tricyclic antidepressants, sedating antihistamines and some antipsychotics, and is associated with cognitive impairment, falls, constipation and urinary retention. Oxybutynin has the highest central nervous system penetration of the bladder antimuscarinics and is generally avoided in older people, with mirabegron preferred if pharmacotherapy is still needed after conservative measures. Non pharmacological treatment remains first line and includes bladder training with timed voiding, pelvic floor muscle training, caffeine reduction and treatment of constipation. Topical vaginal oestrogen improves urgency, frequency and recurrent urinary infection in women with atrophic changes without meaningful systemic absorption.
key_points: Review anticholinergic burden across all drug classes before escalating overactive bladder treatment
Oxybutynin has the highest central penetration of the antimuscarinics and is avoided in older people
Bladder training, pelvic floor training and constipation management remain first line at any age
Topical vaginal oestrogen improves urgency and frequency in women with an atrophic vaginal mucosa
A raised post void residual suggests impaired emptying and argues against further antimuscarinic therapy
explanation.pearls: Mirabegron is the preferred pharmacological option when an older woman still needs bladder medication, since it acts through beta three agonism rather than muscarinic blockade, though it requires blood pressure monitoring because it can raise it.

subtopic_detail: Vaginal bulge reaching the hymen with dragging discomfort in a woman who declines surgery while caring for her husband
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a sixty eight year old woman who describes a feeling of something coming down in the vagina, worst by the end of the day and when she lifts her grandchildren. She has a dragging discomfort but no urinary or bowel symptoms.

She had three vaginal births and has been postmenopausal for sixteen years. She is the full time carer for her husband, who has advanced Parkinson disease, and tells you she cannot contemplate several weeks of recovery from an operation while he depends on her. She has no bleeding and her cervical screening is up to date.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29 kg/m2, anterior vaginal wall descending to the level of the hymen on Valsalva, cervix descending to within 2 cm of the hymen, posterior wall well supported, vaginal mucosa thin and pale, no ulceration of the exposed epithelium, pelvic floor contraction weak
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative, post void residual 40 mL on bladder scan

options.text: Refer for vaginal hysterectomy with anterior repair and explain that this offers the most durable long term result
options.rationale: Surgery offers durable correction but the woman has clearly stated that a recovery period is not currently feasible given her caring responsibilities. Recommending it first disregards the constraint that actually governs her choice. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

options.text: Advise observation with reassurance, since prolapse at this level rarely progresses and causes no lasting harm
options.rationale: Observation is appropriate for asymptomatic prolapse found incidentally, but this woman has daily dragging discomfort that limits her activity. Reassurance alone leaves a treatable symptom untreated. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

options.text: Prescribe a course of oral oestrogen with progestogen to restore vaginal tissue quality and improve the support
options.rationale: Systemic hormone therapy does not correct anatomical descent and exposes her to unnecessary risk sixteen years after menopause. Topical vaginal oestrogen has a role alongside a pessary for mucosal quality, but it is an adjunct rather than the treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

options.text: Refer for laser or radiofrequency vaginal tightening treatment as a non surgical alternative to a formal repair
options.rationale: Energy based vaginal devices are not supported by adequate evidence for prolapse and have attracted specific safety warnings from regulators including the Therapeutic Goods Administration. Offering them would substitute an unproven intervention for an effective one. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

options.text: Arrange fitting of a vaginal pessary with topical oestrogen and referral for pelvic floor muscle training
options.rationale: A pessary is the first line non surgical treatment for symptomatic prolapse, gives immediate symptom relief without recovery time, and suits a woman who cannot step away from caring duties. Topical oestrogen improves mucosal quality and reduces erosion risk, while pelvic floor training addresses the weak contraction demonstrated on examination. (Source: RANZCOG: Pelvic organ prolapse)

explanation.summary: Pelvic organ prolapse is graded by the relationship of the leading edge to the hymen, and treatment is driven by symptoms and by the woman's circumstances rather than by the stage alone. Asymptomatic prolapse requires no treatment, while symptomatic prolapse is managed with pelvic floor muscle training for milder degrees, a vaginal pessary, or surgery. Pessaries relieve symptoms immediately, avoid operative and anaesthetic risk, and can be used indefinitely or as a bridge to later surgery, which makes them particularly valuable for women who cannot accept a recovery period. Ring and ring with support pessaries are the usual first choices, with shelf or Gellhorn devices for more advanced descent. Topical vaginal oestrogen is commonly prescribed alongside to improve mucosal integrity and reduce the risk of erosion, and regular review every three to six months is required to check for ulceration.
key_points: Treatment is driven by symptoms and by the woman's circumstances rather than by the stage alone
A vaginal pessary gives immediate relief with no recovery period and may be used indefinitely
Topical vaginal oestrogen improves mucosal quality and reduces the risk of pessary related erosion
Regular review every three to six months is needed to inspect for ulceration of the vaginal wall
Energy based vaginal devices lack evidence for prolapse and carry regulatory safety warnings
explanation.pearls: A woman with a previously comfortable pessary who develops new vaginal bleeding or discharge should be examined promptly for mucosal erosion, since an untreated erosion can progress to fistula formation over months.

sources.label: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Pelvic floor

subtopic_detail: Oncogenic human papillomavirus not types sixteen or eighteen with a negative reflex liquid based cytology result
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a thirty four year old woman's cervical screening result. She attended for a routine test having had a negative screening result five years earlier, and she has no abnormal bleeding, no discharge and no pain.

She has two children, uses a copper intrauterine device for contraception and has never smoked. She received the human papillomavirus vaccine as part of the school programme in year eight. She is not immunosuppressed and has had no previous abnormal result.

data_table.Examination: Cervix appears normal on speculum examination with no visible lesion, no contact bleeding, intrauterine device threads visible
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test reports oncogenic human papillomavirus detected, not type sixteen or eighteen, with reflex liquid based cytology showing negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for colposcopy within eight weeks because any oncogenic human papillomavirus detection requires assessment
options.rationale: Immediate colposcopy is reserved for types sixteen or eighteen, or for any oncogenic type with a cytological prediction of possible or definite high grade change. Referring every detection would flood colposcopy services with transient infections that clear spontaneously. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines)

options.text: Repeat the human papillomavirus test in twelve months and refer for colposcopy if oncogenic types persist
options.rationale: Detection of an oncogenic type other than sixteen or eighteen with negative reflex cytology places her in the intermediate risk group, managed by a repeat test at twelve months because most such infections clear without intervention. Persistence at that repeat indicates established infection and triggers colposcopy referral. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines)

options.text: Return her to routine five yearly screening, since the reflex cytology showed no intraepithelial abnormality
options.rationale: Negative cytology reduces but does not eliminate risk, because cytology has limited sensitivity for a single time point and the infection may yet persist. A five year interval is too long for a woman with a detected oncogenic type. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines)

options.text: Repeat the screening test in six months and refer for colposcopy only if the cytology becomes abnormal as well
options.rationale: A six month interval is too short to allow transient infection to clear and is not the interval the programme specifies. Making referral conditional on cytology also misses the women whose persistent infection has not yet produced cytological change. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines)

options.text: Offer the nonavalent human papillomavirus vaccine now to help clear the infection that has been detected
options.rationale: Vaccination is prophylactic and does not clear an infection that is already established, so it cannot substitute for surveillance. It may still be discussed for protection against types she has not yet encountered, but it does not change this result's follow up. (Source: NCIRS: Australian Immunisation Handbook)

explanation.summary: The Australian National Cervical Screening Program uses a primary human papillomavirus test every five years from twenty five to seventy four, with reflex liquid based cytology performed on the same sample when an oncogenic type is detected. Results fall into three risk categories that determine management. Higher risk means detection of type sixteen or eighteen, or any oncogenic type with cytology predicting possible or definite high grade squamous or glandular change, and these women are referred for colposcopy. Intermediate risk means an oncogenic type other than sixteen or eighteen with negative or low grade cytology, managed by repeat testing at twelve months since most such infections clear. Lower risk means no oncogenic type detected, returning the woman to five yearly screening, and self collection is available to all screening participants as an equivalent option that improves participation.
key_points: Primary human papillomavirus testing runs five yearly from age twenty five to seventy four
Types sixteen or eighteen prompt direct colposcopy referral regardless of the cytology result
Other oncogenic types with negative or low grade cytology are repeated at twelve months
Persistence of an oncogenic type at the twelve month repeat triggers colposcopy referral
Most infections with oncogenic types clear spontaneously within one to two years
explanation.pearls: Any woman with abnormal vaginal bleeding, postcoital bleeding or a visibly suspicious cervix is investigated on those symptoms regardless of a negative screening result, because screening tests are designed for asymptomatic women and do not exclude cancer.

subtopic_detail: Deep dyspareunia with cervical motion tenderness and a negative pregnancy test in a woman with a recent new partner
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a twenty three year old woman with five days of lower abdominal pain, deep pain with intercourse and an increased vaginal discharge. She has had a new sexual partner for two months and uses condoms inconsistently.

She describes the pain as constant and bilateral, worse on movement. Her last menstrual period was two weeks ago and was normal. She has no urinary symptoms, no vomiting and has been eating normally. She has no history of pelvic surgery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bilateral lower abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound, mucopurulent cervical discharge with contact bleeding on speculum examination, marked cervical motion tenderness with bilateral adnexal tenderness, no adnexal mass palpable
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, urinalysis negative for nitrites and leucocytes, endocervical swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea sent, transvaginal ultrasound shows normal ovaries with no tubo ovarian collection and no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics until the endocervical swab results are available, providing analgesia and review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Treatment is started empirically on clinical criteria because delay increases the risk of tubal damage, infertility and ectopic pregnancy, and a substantial proportion of cases have no organism identified. Waiting for a result that may be negative would leave the tubes inflamed for several more days. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

options.text: Prescribe oral trimethoprim for five days and arrange a midstream urine culture with review if symptoms persist
options.rationale: Urinary tract infection would produce dysuria and frequency with an abnormal urinalysis rather than cervical motion tenderness and mucopurulent cervical discharge. Trimethoprim does not cover the organisms responsible for upper genital tract infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit for intravenous antibiotics and surgical review, given the fever and the degree of adnexal tenderness
options.rationale: Admission is indicated for severe illness, a tubo ovarian abscess, pregnancy, inability to tolerate oral therapy or failed outpatient treatment, none of which apply to a systemically well woman with a reassuring scan. Outpatient oral therapy is as effective for mild to moderate disease. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

options.text: Prescribe oral doxycycline alone for fourteen days and advise that her partner be tested before any treatment
options.rationale: Doxycycline covers chlamydia and some other organisms but leaves gonorrhoea and anaerobes untreated, and single agent therapy is not adequate for polymicrobial upper tract infection. Partners are treated empirically rather than only after a positive test, because delay allows reinfection. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

options.text: Give intramuscular ceftriaxone now with oral doxycycline and metronidazole for fourteen days, and treat her partner
options.rationale: Lower abdominal pain with cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness in a sexually active young woman meets the minimum criteria for pelvic inflammatory disease, which is treated empirically with cover for gonorrhoea, chlamydia and anaerobes. Concurrent partner treatment prevents reinfection and is part of the standard Australian regimen. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Pelvic inflammatory disease is diagnosed clinically and treated empirically because the consequences of delay are disproportionate to the cost of treating uncertain cases. The minimum criteria are lower abdominal pain with cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness in a sexually active woman once pregnancy and other causes have been considered, and additional support comes from fever, mucopurulent discharge, raised inflammatory markers or a positive swab. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea are the classical pathogens but many cases are polymicrobial or have no organism identified, so regimens cover all three groups including anaerobes. Australian outpatient treatment combines intramuscular ceftriaxone with oral doxycycline and metronidazole for fourteen days. Untreated or repeatedly treated disease carries cumulative risks of tubal factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain, which rise with each episode.
key_points: Minimum criteria are pelvic pain with cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness in a sexually active woman
Treatment is empirical because delay increases tubal damage, infertility and ectopic pregnancy risk
Australian outpatient therapy is ceftriaxone with doxycycline and metronidazole for fourteen days
Concurrent partner treatment is part of the regimen and prevents rapid reinfection
Admission is for severe illness, tubo ovarian abscess, pregnancy or failure of oral therapy
explanation.pearls: Right upper quadrant pain with pelvic inflammatory disease suggests Fitz Hugh Curtis syndrome, a perihepatitis producing violin string adhesions between liver capsule and diaphragm, which responds to the same antibiotic regimen rather than requiring separate treatment.

subtopic_detail: Cycles of forty to ninety days with a normal semen analysis and patent tubes after fourteen months of trying to conceive
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a twenty eight year old woman who has been trying to conceive for fourteen months. Her periods come every forty to ninety days and have done so since her teens.

She has noticed coarse hair on her chin and upper lip which she waxes fortnightly. Her weight has been stable for two years. Her partner's semen analysis was normal and a hysterosalpingogram performed last month showed both tubes patent with normal uterine contour. She has never smoked and takes folic acid daily.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 31 kg/m2, waist circumference 94 cm, terminal hairs over chin and upper lip, no acanthosis nigricans, no striae, no galactorrhoea, normal visual fields to confrontation, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), prolactin 320 mIU/L (less than 500), follicle stimulating hormone 5.8 IU/L, luteinising hormone 12.4 IU/L, total testosterone 2.8 nmol/L (0.5-1.7), day 21 progesterone 4 nmol/L on two occasions, pelvic ultrasound shows twenty four follicles in one ovary with normal endometrium

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment to help her conceive?

options.text: Prescribe letrozole for ovulation induction with cycle monitoring, alongside advice on weight and lifestyle
options.rationale: Letrozole is first line for ovulation induction in anovulatory polycystic ovary syndrome in current Australian and international recommendations, achieving higher live birth rates than clomiphene, and the low day 21 progesterone confirms anovulation as the barrier. Lifestyle measures run alongside rather than instead of induction, since a modest weight reduction improves both ovulatory and treatment response. (Source: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG)
source_refs: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG

options.text: Prescribe metformin as a single agent and review her cycle regularity after six months of continuous treatment
options.rationale: Metformin improves cycle regularity and metabolic parameters and has an adjunctive role, particularly with a raised body mass index, but as monotherapy it is inferior to letrozole for live birth. Using it alone would spend six months on the weaker option. (Source: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG)
source_refs: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG

options.text: Refer directly for in vitro fertilisation given the fourteen month history and the documented ovulatory failure
options.rationale: In vitro fertilisation is third line for this indication and is considered after ovulation induction and gonadotrophin therapy have failed, since most women with this condition conceive with simpler treatment. Referring now exposes her to cost and procedural risk unnecessarily. (Source: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG)
source_refs: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG

options.text: Prescribe a combined oral contraceptive for three months to regulate her cycles before attempting conception again
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception manages hyperandrogenic symptoms and endometrial protection in women not seeking pregnancy, and it actively prevents the conception she is seeking. It does not improve subsequent ovulation once stopped. (Source: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG)
source_refs: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG

options.text: Refer for laparoscopic ovarian drilling as a durable way to restore spontaneous ovulation over several cycles
options.rationale: Ovarian drilling is a second line option for women who are resistant to or intolerant of oral agents, and it carries surgical risks including adhesion formation and reduced ovarian reserve. It is not offered before an oral induction agent has been tried. (Source: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG)
source_refs: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG

explanation.summary: Polycystic ovary syndrome is diagnosed in adults when two of three criteria are met, namely oligo or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound, after exclusion of thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia and congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Anti Mullerian hormone may now substitute for ultrasound morphology in adults, and ultrasound is not used for diagnosis within eight years of menarche because multifollicular ovaries are normal in adolescence. For women seeking pregnancy, anovulation is the barrier and ovulation induction is the treatment, with letrozole established as first line ahead of clomiphene on live birth rates. Metformin is adjunctive, particularly with obesity or insulin resistance, while gonadotrophins and laparoscopic ovarian drilling are second line and in vitro fertilisation third. Weight reduction of five to ten per cent independently improves ovulatory function and response to induction.
key_points: Diagnosis requires two of anovulation, hyperandrogenism and polycystic morphology after exclusions
Letrozole is first line for ovulation induction and outperforms clomiphene for live birth
Metformin is adjunctive rather than a stand alone fertility treatment in this setting
Gonadotrophins and ovarian drilling are second line, with in vitro fertilisation third
A five to ten per cent weight reduction improves ovulation and the response to induction
explanation.pearls: Ultrasound morphology cannot be used to diagnose polycystic ovary syndrome within eight years of menarche, because multifollicular ovaries are a normal finding in adolescence and applying adult criteria overdiagnoses the condition in teenagers.

sources.label: International PCOS Guideline endorsed by RANZCOG
